01-what-is-vericoding/title.transcript: Ferry coding is a way of writing software where the specification, the proof and the program are all one artifact, checked by a machine.

01-what-is-vericoding/sampling.transcript: Normally, we test. A test runs the program on a handful of inputs, and we hope the rest behave. A specification is different. It says something about every possible input, and a proof is a certificate that the code meets it. Tests sample. Proofs quantify.

01-what-is-vericoding/three-things.transcript: So a very coded program is three things at once. The code, a statement of what that code must mean, and a proof, machine-checked step-by-step, that the code meets the statement. One language for all three, so the specification cannot drift away from the implementation.

01-what-is-vericoding/why-now.transcript: Why now? Proving used to be the bottleneck. A theorem prover could check everything, but writing the proofs took specialists far longer than writing the code. Large language models change the economics. Routine obligations get discharged. Lemmas get suggested. Broken proofs get repaired. The proof is no longer the expensive part.

01-what-is-vericoding/intent.transcript: That moves the scarce resource. The machine cannot invent what your programme must mean. You iterate at the specification surface, in conversation, and the implementation becomes something you can replace later. The dialectic is about intent, not operation.

01-what-is-vericoding/closing.transcript: Next, why a proof is literally a program.

02-proofs-are-programs/title.transcript: A theorem prover is a programme that checks proofs. Everything else follows from how seriously it takes that job.

02-proofs-are-programs/kernel.transcript: You state a claim, you give a proof and a small trusted programme, the Colonel, verifies every step. Nothing is taken on authority. A proof is a certificate. The checker accepts it or it does not. Keeping the Colonel small is what makes it worth trusting.

02-proofs-are-programs/curry-howard.transcript: The reason this can be a programming language is a correspondence. A proposition is a type and a proof is a program of that type. Implication is a function. Conjunction is a pair. Disjunction is a tagged union. For all is a dependent function and there exists is a witness paired with a proof about it.

02-proofs-are-programs/dependent.transcript: that gives types which talk about values. Here is a vector, a list whose type records its length. The head of a non-empty vector has no empty case to handle, because an empty vector cannot have that type. Calling it on nothing is a type error, not an exception.

02-proofs-are-programs/same-machine.transcript: So checking a proof is type checking a program. The proof assistant and the compiler are the same machine. That is what lets one language carry the program, the specification, and the proof.

03-first-contract/title.transcript: A contract is a theorem about a definition. Here is the smallest one worth writing.

03-first-contract/program.transcript: Here is a very small program. Maxoff returns the larger of two natural numbers. It is correct, but nothing about it says so.

03-first-contract/statement.transcript: The specification is another term in the same language. For all a and b, a is at most max of ab. That is a statement about every pair of numbers, not a sample.

03-first-contract/proof.transcript: The proof is a program of that statement's type. We unfold the definition, split on the comparison, and in each branch, the arithmetic closes the goal. Lean prints the goal state after every step, so the proof is not a story about the code. It is the machine's own working.

03-first-contract/errors.transcript: Two kinds of error now become visible. An error of reasoning, connecting things wrongly, is rejected. The kernel will not accept the step. An error of interpretation, misunderstanding what the code means, leaves an artifact. The specification you wrote is there to be read and iterated on.

03-first-contract/closing.transcript: The proof is checked, not reviewed. Next two ways to specify.

04-two-ways-to-specify/title.transcript: There are two ways to attach a claim to code and two ways to embed a language in a prover. Both distinctions matter.

04-two-ways-to-specify/intrinsic.transcript: Intrinsic Specification puts the claim in the type. Here the caller supplies evidence that the list is not empty, so the function has no empty case. Illegal states become unrepresentable, and every caller gets the guarantee for free. The cost is that types get heavier and evidence gets threaded through signatures.

04-two-ways-to-specify/extrinsic.transcript: Extrinsic specification writes the plain program, then states a separate theorem about it. Double is just addition, and the theorem says it equals two times its argument. The program stays idiomatic and the specification can grow by accretion. The cost is that you have to find the right theorems.

04-two-ways-to-specify/rule.transcript: A rule of thumb. Use intrinsic specification for shape, lengths, non-emptiness, invariance of a data structure. Use extrinsic specification for behaviour, what a sort returns, what a file contains after a write, what a protocol did.

04-two-ways-to-specify/deep.transcript: There is a second axis. A deep embedding makes the language understudy into data inside the prover, with the semantics and a theory built about it. Iris does this for concurrent and unsafe programs. Interaction trees do it for effects. It buys reusable reasoning about hard semantics, and it costs you the embedding and its theory.

04-two-ways-to-specify/shallow.transcript: A shallow embedding does not model the language, it uses it. The prover is the programming language. Terms are programs, types are specifications, and proofs are terms checked by the same kernel. There is no gap between the code you reason about and the code that runs.

04-two-ways-to-specify/closing.transcript: This tutorial takes the shallow path. Next, what happens to the proofs when the code compiles?

05-from-proof-to-binary/title.transcript: A proof is a static claim. What comes out of the compiler is a program with no prover in it.

05-from-proof-to-binary/erasure.transcript: Compilation erases whatever exists only for the proof. Proofs are propositions, and propositions carry no runtime data. What is left is the algorithm and its data. The guarantees are static, so nothing is rechecked at runtime, and the cost of having them is zero.

05-from-proof-to-binary/compiler.transcript: Lean elaborates to its own intermediate representation, emits C, and links a small runtime into a native binary. Memory is managed by reference counting rather than a tracing collector, so destruction is deterministic and a uniquely owned value can be updated in place.

05-from-proof-to-binary/measurement.transcript: In this tutorial's own measurement, the extracted sort compiled to a small binary produced byte-identical output and ran about 27 times faster than interpreting the same file.

05-from-proof-to-binary/staircase.transcript: Zoom out, and the whole design is a staircase. Within a level, you optimize. Rewrite the program, keep its behavior. Between levels, you lower. A source language becomes a simpler one, and eventually, machine code. Every vertical edge carries a refinement proof. This stack is a proposed architecture, not a settled result.

05-from-proof-to-binary/closing.transcript: Next, what a verified program still has to assume about the world.

06-building-the-world/title.transcript: A verified programme still has to talk to a world nobody verified. The question is, what it is allowed to assume.

06-building-the-world/effects.transcript: Effects do not disappear. They become explicit. IO is a type and a function that prints says so in its signature. Pure looking code can still run at imperative speed. An array is a value in the type system and a mutable buffer in the implementation, updated in place when it is uniquely owned.

06-building-the-world/binding.transcript: Real programs need the world. Files, sockets, databases, time. Lean can call almost anything, so a binding is a few lines. But a binding is not a library you can verify against. A binding says how to call, a theory says what the call means, and contracts are written against the meaning.

06-building-the-world/axioms.transcript: Every theory ends in an assertion. The operating system, the network card, the database are not vericoded. So the bottom of the stack is exactly what you assume. Keep the assumptions small, explicit, and testable. Differential testing against the real system, property-based checks, fuzzing at the boundary.

06-building-the-world/order.transcript: What to build first, rank by dependence, then by purity. Files first, because everything sits on them, and specify the failures, not only the successes. Then text. Unicode and regular expressions are pure, so they can be proved end to end. Then time, with the wall clock may jump as an explicit axiom. Then JSON and the wire formats.

06-building-the-world/closing.transcript: VeriCoding moves the work to the surface where a machine can check it, what the programme must mean, write the specification, let the proof be checked.

01-what-is-vericoding/opener.transcript: Cydonia Ltd presents Veracoding, an introduction in six parts.
